paras: The threatened lynching of Mat Kimble took place at New Braunfels, Texas, in early July 1903, when armed posses and then a crowd of several hundred people sought a Black man accused of attacking Mrs. Emil Gronle, a farmer's wife, on June 30. Kimble was captured on July 4 and, after a crowd at New Braunfels demanded him the next day, was taken to San Antonio in a woman's dress under militia guard. Papers across the country ran a wire report predicting a lynching, while later San Antonio reports raised doubts about Kimble's guilt.

A telephone report from New Braunfels on June 30 said the wife of Emil Grundel had been raped and murdered about five miles from town by a man "supposed to be a small negro with a mustache." An Associated Press dispatch that night named her Mrs. Gronle and said a man had demanded money, thrown her to the floor and slashed her abdomen with a razor; it called the crime an attempted assault and said she was still alive.

A posse of about forty citizens took up the hunt with bloodhounds from San Antonio, and one version of the wire said "the leaders of the posse say that the negro, if captured, will be burned to death." In San Antonio on July 1 the Daily Light reported a belief that if citizens caught the fugitive before officers he would be lynched "with out ceremony." Several Black men were arrested and released, and that night a crowd at the Bexar County jail talked of taking out and lynching a suspect it believed was inside.

On Saturday, July 4, Deputy Sheriff Lum Stokes of Guadalupe County and Constable Mat Hutchen found Kimble hiding in a cane patch near Fentress, Caldwell County, after trailing him from near the scene. Officers moved him from Seguin to New Braunfels overnight because of "mob sentiment"; on July 5 a crowd that a militia soldier put at some 500 gathered at the jail and demanded him. Officers dressed Kimble in a woman's dress and bonnet and walked him to the depot, where, according to the New Braunfels correspondent, cries of "Mob him!" and "Burn him" were heard, "but there was no one to lead and no organization." The militia company under Captain M. E. Guinn put him on the train and he was turned over to Sheriff John Tobin in San Antonio.

Kimble denied his guilt, but after officers placed a Black detective, Sandy Williams, in his cell he made a statement that he had stabbed the woman with a pocket knife, which he withdrew that night. Governor S. W. T. Lanham ordered Tobin to hold the "Comal county prisoner charged with rape until further orders." A volunteer, J. C. Burt, returned on July 8 with sworn affidavits said to place Kimble 25 miles from the scene.

Mrs. Gronle died, by a later account on the Friday after the attack. At a habeas corpus hearing on August 4, none of the seventeen witnesses heard could positively identify Kimble, and he was ordered held until further orders of the court. No report of an indictment, trial or release was found.

The San Antonio Daily Light covered the case most closely, moving from a "RAPE AND MURDER" headline that called the attacker "the fiend" to "NEGRO DENIES HIS GUILT." Elsewhere the wire ran on July 1 under headlines such as "WITH BLOODHOUNDS NEGRO IS CHASED IN TEXAS" in the Savannah Morning News and "LYNCHING PROBABLE" in the Courier-Journal. Weekly news summaries later reported a murder "by an unknown negro."

The only Black-press account found was in the Savannah Tribune, which on July 4 printed the wire text under "CUT ALMOST IN TWAIN" without comment, in the same item as a report headed "CRUM APPROVES LYNCHINGS." The same text ran in the white Gainesville Star three days later.

The first report called the crime rape and murder, the wire an attempted assault with a razor, and a New Braunfels deputy dispelled the rape report; a rumor also blamed a white man disguised as a Black man. The governor called Kimble a Comal County prisoner, while court reports placed the Gronle farm in Guadalupe County.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Mat Kimble
bases: Armed posses hunted the accused with threats to lynch or burn him (A3, A14), and after his capture a crowd of several hundred demanded him at New Braunfels before militia escorted him away; no one was killed (A11, A12).

The manhunt is reported by the local telephone report and the AP wire in white and Black papers (A1, A3, A10), and the crowd at New Braunfels by both a militia soldier's account and the New Braunfels correspondent (A11, A12).

accounts.label: First local report
accounts.gist: A telephone report from New Braunfels called the crime rape and murder and blamed 'a small negro with a mustache'.

accounts.label: AP wire
accounts.gist: A man demanded money, threw Mrs. Gronle down and slashed her with a razor; she was alive; he would probably be lynched, or, in one version, burned, if caught.

accounts.label: Militia soldier
accounts.gist: Some 500 people demanded the prisoner, and the troops had to fight their way to the train; a half hour's delay might have cost Kimble his life.

accounts.label: New Braunfels correspondent
accounts.gist: A few cried 'Mob him!' and 'Burn him' but there was no leader; the crowd asked to keep Kimble in the local jail and was 'cool and collected'.

accounts.label: Officers' confession claim
accounts.gist: Officers said Kimble confessed to a planted cellmate and then to them, using a pocket knife; Kimble recanted that night, saying Williams had held out hopes.

accounts.label: Alibi affidavits
accounts.gist: Volunteer J. C. Burt's sworn statements were said to place Kimble 25 miles away at the hour of the crime.

framing.detail: The San Antonio Daily Light opened with 'RAPE AND MURDER' and 'The Fiend,' then printed the deputy's denial of rape, the recantation and the alibi 'proofs'.
Out-of-state papers ran the AP dispatch under headlines such as 'WITH BLOODHOUNDS NEGRO IS CHASED IN TEXAS' and 'LYNCHING PROBABLE', and news summaries reported a murder 'by an unknown negro'.
The Savannah Tribune printed the wire text 'CUT ALMOST IN TWAIN' without comment, in the same item as a report on W. D. Crum's remarks on lynching.

conflicts.note: The confession was obtained through a planted cellmate and recanted the same night (A11).
Location also varies: five miles southeast of New Braunfels (A3) vs four miles west (A23).
June 10 in A23 appears to be a misprint; all contemporaneous reports date the attack June 30.

info: Attack on Mrs. Gronle and start of manhunt Tuesday, June 30, 1903; capture Saturday, July 4; crowd at New Braunfels and transfer to San Antonio Sunday, July 5
Gronle farm about five miles (southeast) of New Braunfels; capture near Fentress, Caldwell County; crowd at the New Braunfels jail and I. & G. N. depot
Mat Kimble, Black, about 20 or 25 years old, accused; other Black men arrested and released as suspects during the search

Accused of attacking Mrs. Emil (Annie) Gronle at her farm home: first reported as rape and murder, then as attempted assault and a razor wound to the abdomen after demanding money; later charged with criminal assault and murder
Posses of armed citizens with bloodhounds; a crowd at New Braunfels that demanded the prisoner
Kimble was not lynched; held in the Bexar County jail; final disposition not found
